4840:
The surviving text begins mid-conversation: the risen Saviour teaches that matter will dissolve back into its roots, that "there is no sin" in itself but people create sin by mixing with the wrong nature, and that the Son of Man is within them. He sends them to preach and departs. The disciples weep, afraid they will be killed like him. Mary comforts them, and at Peter's request tells what the Lord showed her in a vision: the soul rises past four powers - Darkness, Desire, Ignorance and Wrath, which has seven forms - answering each one and winning freedom. Andrew says these teachings are strange; Peter asks whether the Saviour really spoke privately with a woman and preferred her to them. Mary weeps; Levi rebukes Peter as hot-tempered and says the Saviour knew her well and loved her more than them. They go out to preach.

Pages 1-6 and 11-14 are lost. The Coptic text is in the Berlin Codex (Papyrus Berolinensis 8502), bought in Cairo in 1896 and published only in 1955. Two Greek fragments from the third century (P.Rylands 463 and P.Oxy. 3525) show it was being copied in Egypt early. Its exact religious setting is debated: it is often grouped with Gnostic texts, but it lacks a full Gnostic myth.

4847: It is a second-century work, not written by Mary Magdalene, with no apostolic link, and it was little known in antiquity: no early church writer clearly mentions it. Its teaching that matter will dissolve, that sin is not a real thing, and that salvation is the soul's escape from cosmic powers conflicts with the apostolic gospel of a bodily resurrection and forgiveness of sins. Some modern scholars, such as Karen King, argue that its marginalisation also reflects conflicts over women's authority; others reply that its theology, not its heroine, explains why it was never read as Scripture.
4848: It is the only early Gospel named after a woman and gives Mary Magdalene a leading role as teacher and comforter. It shows that second-century Christians argued about whether revelation could come through private visions and through women. It is widely read today in discussions about women in church leadership and in recovering Mary Magdalene from the later (sixth-century Western) confusion of her with a repentant prostitute.
4849: Named after Mary; not written by her or any apostle.
4850: Denies the reality of sin as such and teaches the soul's escape from matter.
4853: Presents Mary's private vision as revelation from the Saviour.
4855: No surviving church father clearly names or quotes the Gospel of Mary; it is known from manuscripts only.

4859: Mary Magdalene among the women who travelled with Jesus.

4872: The Gospel of Philip is not a story of Jesus but a collection of Valentinian Gnostic reflections on sacraments, names, and spiritual marriage, found at Nag Hammadi in 1945. It is famous for a damaged line saying Jesus kissed Mary Magdalene, which novels like *The Da Vinci Code* turned into a claim that they were married. Scholars read it as symbolic teaching about the "bridal chamber" sacrament.
4873:
The work is an anthology of over a hundred short excerpts - sayings, arguments, metaphors - mostly from the Valentinian school, an influential second-century Christian Gnostic movement. It speaks of five sacraments: baptism, chrism (anointing), eucharist, redemption and the bridal chamber, the highest, in which the soul is united with its heavenly counterpart, healing the separation of male and female that began when Eve was separated from Adam. It plays with names ("Jesus", "Christ", "Nazarene"), claims that those who say the Lord first died and then rose are mistaken, and says Mary Magdalene was the Saviour's companion (koinonos).

The famous passage is full of holes. It says that the companion of [the Saviour] is Mary Magdalene, that he loved her more than the other disciples, and that he used to kiss her often on her [...] - the last word is lost, and "mouth" is only a modern guess. In Valentinian texts a kiss stands for spiritual conception and the giving of grace (elsewhere the same work says the perfect conceive and give birth through a kiss), so most scholars think the passage is symbolic, not a historical report of marriage. The only copy is Nag Hammadi Codex II, copied in the fourth century.

4875: The Lord's mother, the Holy Spirit, and the virgin birth reinterpreted
4876: Mary Magdalene as the Lord's companion; the kiss passage

4880: Truth revealed in types and images
4881: It was never known as a candidate for Scripture: it is late (probably third century), anonymous despite its later title, and a compilation of Valentinian teaching. Its views - that the virgin birth is misunderstood if taken literally, that resurrection must be achieved in this life, and that ordinary believers are of a lower class than the spiritual - were exactly the Valentinian positions Irenaeus and others opposed in the second century.
4882: It is the richest source on Valentinian sacraments and spirituality, showing that many Gnostics were sacramental church-goers, not just philosophers. Its reflections on symbols and names are subtle. Through popular culture it is now the most quoted Nag Hammadi text on Jesus and Mary Magdalene, and scholars use it to explain why the "married Jesus" claim misreads the text.

4909: The Gospel of Truth is a beautiful meditation, more sermon than gospel, on how Jesus brought knowledge of the Father to people lost in forgetfulness and fear. It may have been written by Valentinus, a gifted Christian teacher in Rome in the 140s who founded a Gnostic school. Irenaeus says the Valentinians had a "Gospel of Truth"; copies were found at Nag Hammadi.
4910:
It opens: the gospel of truth is joy for those who have received from the Father the grace of knowing him. Ignorance of the Father produced anguish and terror, and "Error" grew strong, fashioning a substitute for truth like a fog. Jesus came as a teacher and guide; he was nailed to a tree and became fruit of the knowledge of the Father, which gives joy to those who eat it. He put on the living book of the Father and published the Father's edict on the cross. The lost sheep parable is retold with number symbolism (counting to 99 on the left hand, then 100 moves to the right). Those who know are like people waking from a nightmare. All are called by name and return to the Father, the place of rest.

The text survives in Nag Hammadi Codex I (the "Jung Codex", purchased for the Jung Institute in Zurich in 1952) and in fragments in Codex XII. Its style closely resembles what we know of Valentinus' fragments, which is why many think he wrote it, though this cannot be proved. It is gentler than many Gnostic texts and has no detailed myth of evil creator gods.
4911: The gospel of truth is joy; ignorance and Error (opening section)
4912: Jesus the teacher, crucified as fruit of knowledge on the tree

4918: It was not a gospel in the sense of an account of Jesus, had no apostolic author, and was written in the mid-second century, after the four Gospels were already in use. Irenaeus complained that the Valentinians had gone far beyond all limits by calling a recent composition the Gospel of Truth when it agreed in nothing with the apostles' Gospels (*Against Heresies* 3.11.9). Its teaching that salvation is knowledge overcoming ignorance, with sin and the cross treated mainly as error and revelation, differed from the apostolic emphasis on atonement and resurrection.
4919: It is one of the most eloquent early Christian writings from any group and is the best evidence for Valentinian piety, which was deeply focused on the Father's love and Jesus as revealer. Scholars use it to show that Gnostic Christians also used the New Testament heavily - it alludes to Matthew, John, Paul, Hebrews and Revelation - which helps date the authority of those books.

4922: Mild in tone but rooted in Valentinian theology the church rejected.

4946: The Apocryphon of John is the classic Gnostic myth. The risen Christ appears to John and explains that the world was made not by the true God but by a flawed, arrogant being called Yaldabaoth, born from the mistake of a heavenly power called Sophia (Wisdom). Humans carry a spark of divine light that must be awakened. It was so important to Gnostic groups that four copies survive, more than any other Gnostic text.
4947:
After the crucifixion, John, grieving, is challenged by a Pharisee. The Saviour appears to him in changing forms and reveals the hidden truth. Above everything is the invisible, unknowable Spirit, from whom comes Barbelo, the first thought, and a series of aeons. The last aeon, Sophia, tries to produce something without her partner, and gives birth to a misshapen being, Yaldabaoth, who steals some of her light, creates rulers and the material world, and boasts, "I am a jealous God and there is no other God beside me." To recover the light, the higher powers trick him into breathing it into Adam. The rest of Genesis is retold in reverse: the serpent and tree of knowledge become signs of liberation, the flood and the "sons of God" become Yaldabaoth's attempts to keep humanity enslaved. Christ comes as the Providence of light to awaken souls.

It survives in four Coptic copies: three at Nag Hammadi (Codices II, III and IV, in a shorter and a longer version) and one in the Berlin Codex 8502. Irenaeus, around 180, summarises a very similar myth of the "Barbelo-Gnostics" (*Against Heresies* 1.29), showing that a version existed by then.

4955: It teaches what the early church saw as the opposite of the biblical faith: that the God of Israel who created the world is an ignorant or malicious lesser being, that the body and material world are a prison, and that salvation is escape of the spark of light. Irenaeus' whole work *Against Heresies* was aimed at myths like this. It has no apostolic author and dates from the second century at the earliest.
4956: It is the key text for understanding Sethian Gnosticism, the closest thing to a "classic" Gnostic system, and for understanding what Irenaeus and others were arguing against. It is also an early, ambitious attempt to wrestle with the problem of evil and the origin of the world, reading Genesis alongside Plato.

4980: Pistis Sophia is a long, complex Gnostic book in which the risen Jesus, who has stayed with his disciples for eleven years, teaches them about the heavenly realms and the fall and rescue of a heavenly being called Pistis Sophia. Mary Magdalene asks most of the questions, often to Peter's irritation. It was bought by the British Museum in 1785, long before the Nag Hammadi find.
4981:
Eleven years after the resurrection, Jesus is taken up into light and returns to tell his disciples about his journey through the heavens and about Pistis Sophia ("Faith-Wisdom"), who was lured into chaos by a false light and cried out in thirteen songs of repentance. Each repentance is explained by a disciple using a psalm or one of the *Odes of Solomon*. Jesus describes the many treasuries, rulers and places of punishment, and the "mysteries" (rituals) that allow souls to pass upward. Mary Magdalene speaks far more than anyone else and is praised; Peter complains that she dominates, and Jesus encourages everyone with spiritual understanding to speak.

The manuscript, now called the Askew Codex after the London doctor Anthony Askew who owned it, was bought by the British Museum in 1785 and was one of the first Gnostic texts studied in modern times. It is a later Gnostic work, probably third century, with a heavily elaborated system of heavens.

4983: The fall of Pistis Sophia and her thirteen repentances, interpreted through the psalms (Books 1-2)
4985: The mysteries and the fate of souls (Books 3)

4988: It is a late (third-century or later) text with an elaborate Gnostic cosmology that has little in common with the apostolic writings. It was never known or proposed as Scripture by any church. Its extension of the risen Jesus' teaching from forty days to eleven years is a typical Gnostic way of claiming later secret revelation.
4989: It gives a rare view of later Egyptian Gnostic ritual and speculation, preserves Coptic versions of five *Odes of Solomon*, and shows how Gnostic Christians read the Psalms. Its prominent Mary Magdalene and Peter-Mary rivalry link it to the Gospel of Mary and Gospel of Thomas. It also shaped nineteenth- and twentieth-century esoteric movements.
